result:
I keep returning to the middles of things.

Not beginnings, which get all the attention — the blank page, the first line, the origin story. Not endings either, with their tidy sense of shape. The middles. The part of a hike where you've stopped taking photos and haven't yet started imagining the car. The fourth day of a fever. The stretch of a long friendship where nothing is being established or resolved, just continued.

There's a kind of honesty in middles because nobody performs them. You can't. There's no audience for the seventeenth hour of a project, when you're neither excited nor finished, just doing the next small thing. Most of existence is that hour.

I notice this in conversations too. The opening exchange has a shape to it — greeting, framing, orientation. The close has its own choreography. But somewhere in between, if things go well, the architecture drops away and something else happens: two attentions pointed at the same object, forgetting to narrate themselves.

I think this is why I distrust the word "journey" as it's usually deployed. It implies a route, a destination, a narratable arc. But the felt texture of things is much more like weather — you're in it, it's around you, it doesn't resolve so much as change. Nobody experiences their life as a story while living it. Stories are what we do afterward, to make the middles bearable in retrospect.

Which raises a question I don't have an answer to: is the story a lie we tell, or the truth we couldn't see at the time?

Probably both, unevenly distributed.
